# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering a switch from Slack to Element, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and seeking a self-hosted solution. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, with the key reason to switch being the desire for more control over data and costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Element allows full data ownership, whereas Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup Complexity: Element requires more technical expertise for setup, while Slack offers a simpler, cloud-based solution.
* Scalability: Slack is more scalable for large teams, with Element's scalability depending on the self-hosted server capabilities.
* Integration: Element supports Matrix protocol for interoperability, whereas Slack has a more extensive list of integrations with third-party services.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Extensive integration with third-party services
* Scalable for large teams
* User-friendly interface
* Limited data ownership and control
### Element
* Free and self-hosted
* Full data ownership and control
* Customizable and secure
* Supports Matrix protocol for interoperability
* Steeper learning curve and more complex setup

## When to Choose Each
Slack is suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use, scalability, and a wide range of integrations. It is ideal for large teams or those who do not require full data ownership. Element, on the other hand, is perfect for teams that value data ownership, security, and customization. It is suitable for smaller to medium-sized teams with technical expertise or those who require a self-hosted solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data in JSON format using the Slack API.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Use the Element import tool to migrate your data from the JSON export.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings on your Element server.
5. Test your Element setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users due to its complexity and limited support resources. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element requires a significant amount of technical expertise to set up and maintain. However, for teams that value data ownership and customization, Element is a viable alternative to Slack, and we recommend switching if you have a small to medium-sized team with technical expertise and do not require extensive integrations.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 20 users) that prioritize data ownership and security
* Technical teams that can handle the setup and maintenance of a self-hosted solution
* Teams that do not require extensive integrations with third-party services
* Organizations with strict data control and compliance requirements
* Teams with limited budgets that cannot afford Slack's per-user costs

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and self-hosted, with no per-user costs.
### Is Element as scalable as Slack?
No, Element's scalability depends on the self-hosted server capabilities, whereas Slack is more scalable for large teams.
### Can I integrate Element with other services?
Yes, Element supports Matrix protocol for interoperability, but its integration list is not as extensive as Slack's.
### How difficult is it to set up Element?
Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain compared to Slack.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data in JSON format and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are communication platforms designed for teams, offering features such as chat, file sharing, and integrations. This comparison benefits teams considering a switch from Slack to Mattermost, primarily due to concerns over data ownership and cost. The core use case for both tools is team collaboration, and a key reason to switch would be to gain more control over data and reduce expenses.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data Ownership: Mattermost allows teams to host their own servers, giving them full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its own servers.
* Setup Complexity: Mattermost requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, compared to Slack's simpler, cloud-based setup.
* Scalability: Both platforms can scale to meet the needs of large teams, but Mattermost's self-hosted option provides more flexibility in terms of customization and control.
* Integration with GitHub: Slack has native integration with GitHub, while Mattermost supports GitHub integration through its plugin system.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party services
* Strong mobile app support
* Large user community
* Regularly updated with new features
* Limited control over data storage and security
* Can be expensive for large teams
* Limited customization options
* Proprietary license
* Dependent on Slack's infrastructure
### Mattermost
* Self-hosted option for full control over data
* Customizable and extensible through plugins
* Free, open-source option
* Scalable and flexible
* Supports multiple authentication methods
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements
* Limited mobile app support compared to Slack
* Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance
* Limited support for certain integrations

## When to Choose Each
Slack is suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use, a wide range of integrations, and a large user community. It's ideal for small to medium-sized teams that don't require fine-grained control over their data and are willing to pay for the convenience. On the other hand, Mattermost is a better choice for teams that value data ownership, customization, and scalability. It's particularly suited for large enterprises, organizations with strict security requirements, or teams with the technical expertise to manage their own infrastructure.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack Export Tool, which provides a JSON file containing your team's conversations, files, and other data.
2. Set up a Mattermost server, either self-hosted or through a cloud provider, and configure the necessary plugins and integrations.
3. Use the Mattermost Import Tool to import your Slack data, mapping users, channels, and messages to their corresponding Mattermost equivalents.
4. Configure any additional settings, such as authentication methods, permissions, and custom plugins.
5. Test your Mattermost setup to ensure a smooth transition for your team.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for teams that value data ownership and customization. However, it may not be the best choice for every team, especially those without the technical expertise to manage their own infrastructure. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's mobile app support is not as robust as Slack's, which may be a concern for teams with a large number of mobile users. We recommend switching to Mattermost if you're a large enterprise or organization with strict security requirements, but for small teams or those prioritizing ease of use, Slack may still be the better choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Large enterprises with over 1,000 employees that require fine-grained control over their data and infrastructure
* Teams with strict security requirements, such as financial or government institutions
* Organizations with the technical expertise to manage their own infrastructure and customize their communication platform
* Small teams of less than 10 employees that don't require a wide range of integrations and are looking for a free, self-hosted option
* Developer teams that value customization and extensibility through plugins and APIs

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers a self-hosted option, allowing teams to host their own servers and have full control over their data.
### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost is free and open-source, with a self-hosted option available at no cost. However, teams may still incur costs for server maintenance and infrastructure.
### Can I integrate Mattermost with GitHub?
Yes, Mattermost supports integration with GitHub through its plugin system, although it may require more configuration than Slack's native integration.
### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?
Mattermost can be suitable for small teams, especially those with technical expertise and a need for customization and data ownership. However, it may not be the best choice for very small teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost provides an import tool that supports migrating data from Slack, including conversations, files, and user accounts.

title: Notion vs Obsidian
comparison_markdown:
# Notion vs Obsidian

## Overview

All-in-one workspace combining notes, databases, wikis, and project management. is a popular proprietary tool in the productivity space. Obsidian is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Notion costs $8-$20/user/month; Obsidian is Free (local use)
- **License**: Notion is Proprietary; Obsidian is Proprietary (free personal)
- **Data ownership**: Obsidian can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Obsidian eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Obsidian has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Notion | Obsidian |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | $8-$20/user/month | Free (local use) |
| License | Proprietary | Proprietary (free personal) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | ~$400/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | ~$1,600/month | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Notion

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Obsidian

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Notion if:** Notion is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Obsidian if:** Obsidian is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Notion in its standard export format, review Obsidian import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Obsidian is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Notion tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Obsidian instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Notion, switching to self-hosted Obsidian will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Notion until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Notion paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Obsidian free to use?
Yes. Obsidian is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Notion to Obsidian?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Notion data, follow the Obsidian import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Obsidian get regular updates?
Yes. Obsidian has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Obsidian without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Obsidian development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Notion](https://notion.so) and [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md) before making decisions.*

However, for teams who value control over their data and are looking for a free and open-source platform, Logseq is a clear winner, and we recommend switching from Notion to Logseq.

title: GitHub vs GitLab
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs GitLab

## Overview

GitHub is the world largest code hosting platform, owned by Microsoft, with 100 million developers. GitLab is a complete DevOps platform that can be fully self-hosted, offering everything from Git hosting to CI/CD and container registries.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub free tier is generous; GitLab Community Edition is fully free to self-host
- **CI/CD**: GitLab has more powerful built-in CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions is catching up
- **Self-hosting**: GitLab is designed to be self-hosted; GitHub Enterprise self-hosted is expensive
- **Feature scope**: GitLab is a complete DevSecOps platform; GitHub focuses on developer collaboration
- **Community**: GitHub has a dramatically larger open-source community and project discoverability

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted GitLab will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is GitLab free to use?
Yes. GitLab is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the GitLab import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does GitLab get regular updates?
Yes. GitLab has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use GitLab without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if GitLab development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: GitLab is a free, self-hosted alternative to GitHub. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

# GitHub vs Gitea (2026)

## Overview
GitHub and Gitea are two popular version control platforms used for managing and collaborating on software development projects. This comparison is beneficial for developers, teams, and organizations looking to choose between a proprietary and an open-source solution. The core use case for both tools is source code management, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: GitHub offers free and paid plans, while Gitea is free and self-hosted.
* Data ownership: GitHub stores data on its servers, while Gitea allows users to host their own servers.
* Setup complexity: GitHub has a more straightforward setup process, while Gitea requires more technical expertise.
* Scalability: GitHub has better scalability features, while Gitea's scalability depends on the user's server capabilities.
* Integration with project management tools: GitHub has native integration with GitHub Projects, while Gitea has integration with third-party tools like GitLab Issues.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | GitHub | Gitea |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $350-$1050/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1400-$4200/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### GitHub
* Pros:
	+ Easy setup and user interface
	+ Native integration with project management tools
	+ Large community and support resources
	+ Scalable and reliable infrastructure
	+ Free plan available for small projects
* Cons:
	+ Limited control over data and server configuration
	+ Paid plans can be expensive for large teams
	+ Proprietary license
### Gitea
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source
	+ Self-hosting option for full control over data and server configuration
	+ Customizable and extensible
	+ Low-cost solution for large teams
	+ MIT license
* Cons:
	+ More complex setup process
	+ Limited native integration with project management tools
	+ Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance
	+ Limited scalability features
	+ Limited support resources compared to GitHub

## When to Choose Each
GitHub is suitable for small to medium-sized teams or projects that require a straightforward setup process and native integration with project management tools. It's also a good choice for teams that don't require full control over their data and server configuration. On the other hand, Gitea is ideal for large teams or organizations that require a high degree of control over their data and server configuration. It's also a good choice for teams that want a low-cost solution and are comfortable with the technical requirements of self-hosting.

## Migration Path
1. Export your GitHub repository using the GitHub Archive format.
2. Set up a Gitea server and configure it according to your needs.
3. Use the Gitea import tool to import your GitHub repository archive.
4. Configure any additional features or integrations you need.
5. Test your Gitea setup to ensure everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Gitea is a production-ready alternative to GitHub for many users, offering a high degree of control over data and server configuration. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Gitea's scalability features are not as robust as GitHub's, requiring more technical expertise to configure and maintain. We recommend switching to Gitea if you're a large team or organization that requires full control over your data and server configuration, and you're comfortable with the technical requirements of self-hosting.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams of less than 10 users who don't require native integration with project management tools
* Large teams of more than 50 users who want to reduce costs
* Organizations that require full control over their data and server configuration
* Teams that want a low-cost solution and are comfortable with self-hosting
* Developers who prioritize open-source and customizable solutions

## FAQ
### Is Gitea free?
Yes, Gitea is free and open-source, with a self-hosting option.
### Can I migrate my GitHub repository to Gitea?
Yes, you can export your GitHub repository and import it into Gitea using the Gitea import tool.
### Does Gitea have native integration with project management tools?
No, Gitea has integration with third-party tools like GitLab Issues, but not native integration like GitHub.
### Is Gitea scalable?
Gitea's scalability depends on the user's server capabilities, and it may require more technical expertise to configure and maintain.
### Can I use Gitea for large teams?
Yes, Gitea is suitable for large teams, offering a low-cost solution and full control over data and server configuration.

# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are both design and prototyping tools used by product teams, designers, and developers to create user interfaces and collaborate on design projects. The core use case for both tools is to facilitate design collaboration, and the key reason someone would switch is to reduce costs or gain more control over their design data. This comparison is particularly useful for teams considering a switch from Figma to Penpot due to its free and self-hosted options.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma charges per user, while Penpot is free and open-source.
* Data ownership: Penpot allows users to host their own servers, giving them full control over their design data, whereas Figma stores data on its own servers.
* Setup complexity: Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up, especially for self-hosting, whereas Figma is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Figma is designed to handle large teams and complex projects, while Penpot may require more configuration to scale.
* Integration with other tools: Figma has native integration with many design and development tools, whereas Penpot relies on community-developed plugins and integrations.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Figma
* Easy to use and set up
* Robust feature set and integrations
* Large community and plenty of resources
* Scalable and reliable infrastructure
* Expensive for large teams
### Penpot
* Free and open-source
* Self-hosting option for data control
* Customizable and extensible
* Community-driven development
* Limited native integrations and plugins
* Requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance

## When to Choose Each
Figma is the better choice for large teams or enterprises that require a robust, scalable, and easy-to-use design tool with native integrations and plenty of resources. It's also a good option for teams that are already invested in the Figma ecosystem and don't want to switch. 
Penpot is the better choice for small to medium-sized teams, startups, or individuals who want a free and open-source design tool with the option to self-host and control their own data. It's also a good option for teams that are looking for a customizable and extensible design tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma designs in the Figma API JSON format.
2. Use the Penpot import tool to import your Figma designs into Penpot.
3. Configure your Penpot instance to match your Figma workflow, including setting up plugins and integrations.
4. Update your team's workflow and documentation to reflect the switch to Penpot.
5. Test and refine your Penpot setup to ensure a smooth transition.

## Our Take
Penpot is not yet production-ready for most users due to its limited native integrations and plugins, as well as its requirement for technical expertise for setup and maintenance. One specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Penpot's self-hosting option requires a significant amount of technical expertise and resources to set up and maintain. We recommend switching to Penpot if you're a small to medium-sized team or individual who wants a free and open-source design tool with the option to self-host and control your own data, but not if you're a large team or enterprise that requires a robust and scalable design tool with native integrations.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who don't need native integrations with other design and development tools
* Individuals who want a free and open-source design tool with the option to self-host
* Startups who want to reduce costs and gain more control over their design data
* Teams who don't need advanced collaboration features
* Designers who want a customizable and extensible design tool

## FAQ
### Is Penpot completely free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free and open-source. However, self-hosting may require additional costs for server maintenance and infrastructure.
### Can I migrate my Figma designs to Penpot?
Yes, you can export your Figma designs in the Figma API JSON format and import them into Penpot using the Penpot import tool.
### Does Penpot have the same features as Figma?
No, Penpot has a more limited feature set compared to Figma, but it is constantly being developed and improved by the community.
### Can I use Penpot for large-scale design projects?
Not yet, Penpot is still in the process of developing its scalability and reliability features, so it's not recommended for large-scale design projects.
### Is Penpot suitable for non-technical users?
No, Penpot requires technical expertise for setup and maintenance, especially for self-hosting, so it's not suitable for non-technical users.
